query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled surface pre-oxidation treatment, such as plasma oxidation, which forms a thin, dense, and HfO2-enriched oxide layer on the as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, will act as a barrier to oxygen ingress and improve its high‐temperature oxidation resistance without compromising its room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy that exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but is prone to rapid oxidation (pesting) in air at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Apply a surface pre-oxidation treatment using plasma oxidation under controlled conditions to develop a thin, adherent protective oxide scale on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at high temperatures (800–1000 °C) for approximately 5 hours, with the material subsequently subjected to mechanical loading at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin and dense HfO2-enriched oxide scale formed on the surface of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: The preformed oxide layer acts as a diffusion barrier that limits oxygen ingress into the bulk material, thereby preventing or delaying pesting while leaving the internal microstructure and mechanical properties of the alloy largely unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy will show significantly reduced oxidation (less surface degradation) during high-temperature air exposure while maintaining the original levels of tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength, as compared to untreated samples.
generation.baseline: The untreated, as-cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibits rapid oxidation (pesting) under the same high-temperature air exposure conditions, compromising its high-temperature applicability.
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 800–1000 °C, atmosphere of air, exposure time of approximately 5 hours, and mechanical testing performed at strain rates from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹. The intervention must not alter the casting microstructure that provides the beneficial mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how uniform and adherent the oxide scale will be across various processing conditions, and whether the plasma oxidation treatment might inadvertently affect near-surface microstructure in a way that could degrade mechanical properties over longer exposures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr cast samples. Subject one set to the proposed plasma oxidation treatment under controlled conditions optimized to form a thin, uniform HfO2-enriched scale. Expose both treated and untreated samples to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, perform detailed surface characterization (using SEM/EDS and XRD) to assess the oxide scale’s integrity and thickness. Conduct tensile tests at room temperature and at high temperature (1000 °C at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹) to evaluate any variations in mechanical performance.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and continuity (SEM, XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples exhibit oxidation (e.g., similar mass gain, oxide spallation, or pesting behavior) comparable to untreated samples or if the mechanical properties (tensile ductility and/or yield strength) are significantly degraded relative to untreated material, then the hypothesis that the plasma oxidation treatment improves oxygen resistance without compromising mechanical performance will be falsified.

4.1. Phase Stability at High Temperature

HEAs produced on casting when exposed to long-term annealing cause decomposition into the traditional multi-phase microstructure. The alloys decomposition on annealing at a higher temperature creates doubt about its applicability for high-temperature application (over 800 °C). Thermodynamic calculations were performed to understand whether the solid solution established when cast is a thermodynamically stable phase at potential use temperatures. Phase equilibria of CrMnFeCoNi alloy are visualized in Figure 9 as a one-dimensional step diagram of phase fractions and a function of temperature. From Figure 9 the critical features of phase equilibria are readily discernible, such as the thickness of the HEA’s single-phase FCC region (solvus to the solidus) at high temperature from solidus at 1320 °C down to about 750 °C. Also, it shows the lower temperature decomposition products stated in some works. At a lower temperature, phase equilibria show the formation of the sigma phase and BCC phase.

4.1. Oxidation Kinetics and Mechanisms

The presented results showed that the oxidation behavior of the AlNbTiVZr 0.25 refractory high-entropy alloy strongly depends on temperature and time. Particularly, at 600–700 °C, the alloy demonstrated a mixed parabolic-linear rate of the mass gain per unit surface area. The same dependences on the double logarithmic scale revealed two distinct stages of oxidation. During the first stage (0–20 h at 600 °C and 0–5 h at 700 °C), oxidation was slow with n = 0.46–0.48. In turn, the second stage (20–100 h at 600 °C and 5–100 h at 700 °C) was characterized by a significantly faster oxidation rate (n = 0.75–0.72).

Most probably, the acceleration of oxidation at the second stage was caused by an effect similar to breakaway oxidation. frame.system: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy in its unmodified (untreated) state, known to exhibit acceptable mechanical properties at room and high temperatures but suffering from rapid oxygen attack (pesting).
frame.goal: Enhance the oxygen resistance at high temperatures (e.g., 800–1000 °C) without degrading the alloy’s useful room- and high-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength.
frame.limitation: Inadequate oxygen resistance that leads to pesting under high-temperature exposure in air, which currently prevents practical high-temperature applications.
root_cause_cues: does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr
constraints: A single intervention that does not compromise the alloy’s mechanical performance
Preservation of both room-temperature tensile ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C)
Maintaining the cast state of the alloy

regime.loading: Strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1 for high-temperature mechanical performance evaluation

prior_attempts: Earlier oxidation-protection research on a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy successfully prevented pesting during 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C.

Other refractory alloy studies have focused on oxidation resistance but did not evaluate the equiatomic composition or maintain the combination of high mechanical performance with improved oxidation resistance.

decision.trend: Past studies on refractory high‐entropy alloys show two parallel approaches. In one branch, researchers modified composition or processing (e.g., through HIP, ball milling, or minor alloying additions in non‐equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr systems) to promote the formation of secondary phases that can aid in oxidation resistance. In parallel, work on refractory films and related coatings has demonstrated that surface or interface engineering – such as the in‐situ formation of protective oxide layers – can serve as an effective barrier to oxygen ingress without altering the bulk mechanical properties. While bulk compositional or processing modifications sometimes compromise mechanical performance, surface treatments have emerged as a less intrusive means to address oxygen attack.
decision.unsolved: For equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr, the oxidation issue (pesting) under high-temperature exposure (800–1000 °C in air for about 5 hours) remains unresolved. Prior oxidation‐protection work on related (non‐equiatomic) alloys indicates a potential solution, but this specific composition has not yet been safeguarded by any intervention that preserves its beneficial room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
decision.lever: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation or plasma oxidation treatment to form a thin, dense, adherent protective oxide scale (likely enriched in HfO2) on the cast surface
decision.why: A surface protective layer will act as a diffusion barrier to oxygen, thereby mitigating pesting while leaving the internal microstructure—and thus the alloy’s balanced mechanical properties—unaltered. This single-intervention approach aligns with the trend toward minimally intrusive, surface-oriented strategies that have proven effective in related refractory and high-entropy alloy systems.
